article.name: engram (NickCirv)
article.summary: Engram is a local code graph and context tool for coding agents. It indexes source entities and relationships, selected Git and session information, and optional skills into project-local SQLite, then exposes graph retrieval through CLI, hooks, MCP, and a local authenticated HTTP interface.

who_what.text: The official repository presents Engram as a TypeScript/Node project and source-backed CLI/library for local code-graph context, with agent integrations. This review does not infer maintainer identity from account or commit metadata.

architecture.text: The initializer derives .engram/graph.db from a project root and acquires an exclusive init lock. It mines source structure, Git history, reverts, bug-fix commits and session history; optional skills mining and incremental file-mtime skipping are also present.

The sql.js store persists nodes, edges, stats and provider cache. Nodes retain labels, kinds, source file/location, confidence, timestamps, query counts, metadata and optional temporal mistake fields; edges retain relation and source provenance. Save/close exports the in-memory SQLite database.

The repository exposes retrieval through a CLI and library, hooks, MCP and a loopback HTTP interface. Optional providers and integrations can add external processes or network access, so local SQLite does not guarantee every configured workflow stays offline.

behavior.text: Writes use node and edge upserts in SQLite. The core initializer mines graph structure and selected project memory, and the documented public surface includes learn, reindex, watch and mistakes. Upsert replacement is not a complete version history or an auditable correction protocol.

The reviewed README and command reference do not document a general user-facing per-memory delete operation. Low-level SQL availability does not establish a supported targeted deletion workflow; deletion guarantees and post-delete behavior remain unknown.

Retrieval scores text matches on node labels and source files, gives mistake nodes extra weight, searches bounded seed sets and neighbors, starts from the highest-ranked three seeds, then traverses relations and renders within a token budget. The default is BFS depth 3 and 2,000 estimated tokens; rendered character count divided by four is an estimate, not provider token telemetry.

Each project root maps to its own graph path. This separates normal project data locations, but graph rows do not carry a tenant or user access key; no cross-project authorization or hostile local user guarantee was verified. Protected HTTP routes are documented as loopback-bound and authenticated.

Nodes and edges preserve source files/locations, confidence labels/scores, identifiers and timestamps; Git-derived mistakes may retain invalidating-commit and temporal text fields. These are provenance cues, not exact passage citations or independent truth verification.

SQL indexes, per-term search caps, a small seed count, bounded query rendering and cached provider content are implementation controls. Query counters and graph statistics support inspection, but no latency, throughput, token, cost or storage workload was measured.

metrics.evidence: Graph term matching and bounded traversal are implemented; no answer set was scored.
Replacement upserts and temporal mistake fields exist; no correction or stale-value probes were run.
No supported general delete workflow was verified, and no delete or post-delete probe was run.
Per-project paths are implemented; no cross-project isolation workload was run.
Source location and confidence fields exist; no generated claims were adjudicated.
No runtime timing samples were collected.
The query budget is estimated; no resource measurements were collected.

limits.text: This is a source review at the verified current main head. No install, build, runtime, tests, or benchmark execution was performed. Graph retrieval can omit supported-source gaps or return incomplete context; upstream directs users to inspect the original source before relying on a query.

Project-root separation is not a demonstrated security boundary. The documented HTTP interface has authentication controls, while optional integrations may execute processes or access networks. Actual isolation, retrieval correctness, and deletion behavior remain unverified.
Structural context estimates do not establish answer quality or invoice savings. Performance, resource use, and correction/deletion outcomes remain unknown without a versioned measured evaluation.
